cafe.name: Café
cafe.blurb: Food and drink. Daily customers, ingredients, rent, staff and a rival down the road.

expand.label: Open a second café ($60,000)
expand.help: Fit-out and equipment for a second location. It takes a few months to find regulars.

1.title: The coffee cart
1.story: You run a coffee cart outside a busy train station. Each morning you decide your price and how many cups to prepare. Coffee you don’t sell is poured away.
1.text: Have $35,000 in cash by the end of the last month.

2.title: Your first café
2.story: You’ve opened a small café with rent, staff and a menu. New cafés take a few months to be discovered, so expect early losses.
2.text: Make a profit three months in a row before the last month ends, without running out of cash.

3.title: The café across the road
3.story: Commuters, office workers and students all want different things. A few months in, a rival café opens across the road and will react to your prices.
3.text: After the rival opens, make at least $3,000 profit three months in a row.

4.title: Running the books
4.story: Now you see the full picture: equipment that wears out, suppliers you pay a month later, seasons, a bank that will lend, and things that go wrong.
4.text: Reach $60,000 in net cash (cash minus any loan) before the last month ends.

5.title: A second café
5.story: Your café works. Can you grow it into two? You can borrow, bring in an investor, or grow from your own profits.
5.text: Open a second café and make your share of the business worth $300,000.

6.title: Your café, for real
6.story: Everything is switched on: rivals, seasons, events, loans and investors, with bigger month-to-month swings.
6.text: Make your share of the business worth $230,000.

saas.name: Software subscription
saas.blurb: Monthly subscriptions. Sign-ups, cancellations, developers, marketing and investors.

expand.label: Build an enterprise sales team ($15,000)
expand.help: Unlocks sales reps who win large companies on bigger contracts.

1.title: Your first app
1.story: You’ve built a small app that people pay for monthly. About 2,000 people visit your site each month. Choose a price: cheaper wins more sign-ups, but each pays less.
1.text: Reach $12,000 in monthly recurring revenue (MRR) by the last month.

2.title: Growing the startup
2.story: Now you can buy ads and hire developers to improve the product. Better products win more sign-ups and lose fewer customers, but developers are expensive and slow to pay off.
2.text: Have a profitable month with at least $25,000 MRR before the last month ends, without running out of cash.

3.title: Two plans, one rival
3.story: Individuals want cheap; small businesses pay more but expect a better product and support. A few months in, a competitor launches and reacts to your Pro price.
3.text: Reach $30,000 MRR while losing fewer than 4.5% of customers a month.

4.title: Cash is not revenue
4.story: Yearly plans bring cash early but you still owe the service. Seasons, outages, contracts and resignations test you. A bank will lend.
4.text: Reach $50,000 MRR in a profitable month before the last month ends.

5.title: Raise or bootstrap
5.story: Investors value software on recurring revenue and growth. Raise money to grow faster, or keep more of the company and grow on profits.
5.text: Make your share of the company worth $3,000,000.

6.title: Your software company, for real
6.story: Everything is switched on, with bigger swings and more surprises.
6.text: Make your share of the company worth $4,000,000.

shop.name: Online store
shop.blurb: Selling backpacks online. Stock bought ahead, shipping, returns, ads and ratings.

expand.label: Launch a second product line ($25,000)
expand.help: Design and samples for a new range. Brings more visitors once it’s known.

1.title: Your first stock order
1.story: You sell backpacks online. Each month you choose a price and how many bags to buy at $24 each. Bags you don’t sell stay in stock, still holding your cash.
1.text: Have $15,000 in cash by the end of the last month.

2.title: Ads, shipping and returns
2.story: Now you pay for shipping, card fees, storage and returns, and you can buy ads and hire packers. New stores take a few months to be found.
2.text: Make a profit three months in a row before the last month ends, without running out of cash.

3.title: Ratings and rivals
3.story: Bargain hunters and quality seekers want different things. Your star rating decides how many visitors buy. A rival seller appears and fights on price.
3.text: After the rival appears, make at least $2,500 profit three months in a row with a rating of 4.0 or more.

4.title: The holiday rush
4.story: Stock now takes a month to arrive, and you pay your supplier a month later. The holiday season brings huge demand if you have the stock.
4.text: Reach $55,000 in net cash (cash minus any loan) before the last month ends.

5.title: Scaling the store
5.story: Grow with a new product line, a loan or an investor. Online stores sell for roughly 3.4× a year’s earnings.
5.text: Make your share of the business worth $250,000.

6.title: Your store, for real
6.story: Everything is switched on, with bigger swings and more surprises.
6.text: Make your share of the business worth $220,000.

agency.name: Service agency
agency.blurb: A design studio. Billable hours, hourly or fixed prices, and clients who pay late.

expand.label: Open a second studio ($30,000)
expand.help: A second studio in another city. Brings new clients once it’s known.

1.title: Going freelance
1.story: You’re a freelance designer with about 120 billable hours a month. Set your hourly rate: too low and you’re fully booked but poorly paid; too high and the work dries up.
1.text: Have $50,000 in cash by the end of the last month.

2.title: Hiring your first designers
2.story: You rent a studio and can hire designers. Each costs a salary whether or not they have work, so keeping them busy is everything.
2.text: Make a profit three months in a row before the last month ends, without running out of cash.

3.title: Clients and competitors
3.story: Small businesses, startups and corporates want different things. You can charge by the hour or by the project. Cheap freelancers compete for small clients.
3.text: After the rival freelancers appear, make at least $12,000 profit three months in a row.

4.title: Waiting to be paid
4.story: Clients now pay 30 to 60 days after you invoice them. You can be profitable and still run out of cash. Seasons, contracts and staff changes add pressure.
4.text: Reach $120,000 in net cash (cash minus any loan) before the last month ends.

5.title: Building a studio business
5.story: Grow into a second studio, borrow, or bring in a partner investor. Service businesses sell for roughly 2.5× a year’s earnings.
5.text: Open a second studio and make your share of the business worth $900,000.

6.title: Your studio, for real
6.story: Everything is switched on, with bigger swings and more surprises.
6.text: Make your share of the business worth $1,000,000.

4.title: My idea
4.text: Make a profit three months in a row within 24 months, without running out of cash.
